_help: Demo users + seed memory for `node scripts/seed-demo.mjs`. Edit names/ages/grades/styles here and re-run the script. Names are the key: a name that already exists is skipped (learner rows are never changed or deleted); to change an existing user, reset with `SPACETIME_DB=voice-tutor node scripts/publish.mjs --clear` and re-run. Module limits: name 1-40 chars (teacher 1-60), age 5-18, grade 0-13, style max 200 chars. Avoid the 20 simulated students' names (shared/src/classroom/simStudents.ts: Mia Hoffmann, Jonas Becker, ...). `memory` is written with the agent-only reducer seedMemory on every run and REPLACES that student's earlier seeded notes and seed summary (notes the tutor wrote in real sessions are kept): kinds misconception | strategy | mnemonic | quote | understood | preference, outcome worked | didnt | unknown, category/concept from shared/src/lesson/pack/taxonomy.ts, `quote` = the child's words (evidence), mastery 0-100 per concept, `history` = 1-5 earlier sessions (newest = the one the tutor remembers as "last session"), each with `summary`, `nextFocus`, `task`, `concept` (topic) and its own `daysAgo` (distinct); a note's `session` is the index into `history` it was learned in (default: the newest), its quote is shown as said in that session. The old single `summary` (dated `daysAgo`) is still accepted. Notes are listed to the tutor in file order; only notes of the session's topic category (and every preference) are shown.

students.name: Ava Chen
students.demo: self-learning flow (On my own): fractions (task: Expand 2/3 so the bottom number is 12.)

notes.text: When expanding she multiplied only the bottom number: wrote 2/3 = 2/6.
notes.quote: I just times the bottom by 2

notes.text: Cutting every pizza slice into two smaller pieces showed her why the top number has to grow too.
notes.quote: oh, more pieces but it's the same pizza

notes.text: Remembers the rule as "what you do to the bottom, you do to the top".
Knows the bottom number says how many equal pieces the whole is cut into.
notes.quote: the bottom is how many pieces

notes.text: Wants a picture first and only one short hint at a time.

history.task: Expand 2/3 so the bottom number is 6.
history.summary: Ava expanded 2/3 to sixths with a pizza picture. She first multiplied only the bottom (2/6), then fixed it herself after cutting each slice in two (4/6). She is confident about what the bottom number means.
history.nextFocus: Expand 2/3 to twelfths: multiply top and bottom by the same number, picture first.

history.task: A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices. What fraction is one slice, and what are 3 slices?
history.summary: Ava worked on what a fraction is with a pizza cut into 8 slices. With the picture in front of her she named 1/8 and 3/8 and explained that the bottom number says how many equal pieces there are. Long explanations lost her; one short hint at a time worked.
history.nextFocus: Start expanding fractions: the same pizza cut into more pieces.

students.name: Sam Rivera
students.style: step by step, likes to check with numbers
students.demo: self-learning flow (On my own): decimals (task: Which is bigger, 0.3 or 0.25? Explain why.)

notes.text: Compares decimals by the digits after the point: chose 0.35 over 0.4 because 35 is more than 4.
Writing both numbers with the same number of digits (0.40 vs 0.35) let him compare them like whole numbers.
A shaded hundred grid on its own did not convince him; he wanted to check with numbers.
Said "so the zero at the end doesn't change anything" after padding 0.4 to 0.40.
Likes to check an answer with money or a second example before moving on.
Explains the value of each digit in four- and five-digit numbers, zeros included.

history.task: Which is bigger, 0.4 or 0.35? Explain why.
history.summary: Sam compared 0.4 and 0.35 and first chose 0.35 because 35 > 4. Rewriting 0.4 as 0.40 fixed it, and he checked it with money (40 cents vs 35 cents).
history.nextFocus: Compare 0.3 and 0.25 on his own: pad with a zero first, then explain why 0.30 > 0.25.

history.task: What is each digit worth in 3 405?
history.summary: Sam explained the value of every digit in 3 405 and 12 070, including what the zeros mean. He worked step by step and checked each answer by writing it as an amount of money.
history.nextFocus: Move on to decimals: tenths and hundredths as the places after the point.

students.name: Priya Patel
students.style: short sentences, lots of encouragement, pictures first
students.demo: wait-for-teacher flow (joins Ms. Park's class, Class A: adding fractions with the same denominator)

notes.text: Added the tops and the bottoms: 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8.
notes.quote: one and one is two, four and four is eight

notes.text: Colouring pieces of a chocolate bar showed her what 1/4 means.
Can name 1/2, 1/3 and 1/4 from a picture.
Said "the bottom tells how many pieces".
notes.quote: the bottom tells how many pieces

notes.text: Short sentences and a "well done" after each step keep her going; long explanations make her stop answering.

history.task: Colour 1/4 of the chocolate bar. Then what is 1/4 + 1/4?
history.summary: Priya named halves and quarters on a chocolate bar and coloured 1/4 correctly. When adding 1/4 + 1/4 she added the bottoms too (2/8); there was no time left to fix it.
history.nextFocus: Adding fractions with the same denominator: show that the piece size (the bottom number) stays the same.

history.task: Which picture shows 1/2, which 1/3 and which 1/4?
history.summary: Priya matched pictures of halves, thirds and quarters to their fractions and said the bottom tells how many pieces. Short sentences and a "well done" after each step kept her answering.
history.nextFocus: Colour fractions of a chocolate bar, then add two quarters.
